summary.text: At \(n=5\), direct bounds give \(a(5)=4\) and \(a(4)=3\), so the difference is \(1\). But \(k\phi<5\) for \(k\le3\), whereas \(k\phi>6\) for \(k\ge4\), so no positive integer \(k\) has \(\lfloor k\phi\rfloor=5\), contradicting the claimed characterization of positions with difference \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\left\lfloor \frac{n}{\sqrt2}+\frac12\right\rfloor,
\qquad
\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
(The floor is nonnegative for the values in question, so this agrees with the natural-number-valued definition.) Also let
\[
s(m)=\zeta(3)-\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac1{j^3}.
\]
The conjecture is a conjunction. Its second part asserts, in particular, that for every integer \(n\geq 1\),
\[
a(n)-a(n-1)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n=\lfloor k\phi\rfloor\text{ for some integer }k\geq1.
\]
We disprove this equivalence at \(n=5\). The required facts are
\[
a(4)=3,\qquad a(5)=4,
\]
but there is no positive integer \(k\) for which \(\lfloor k\phi\rfloor=5\).

First compute \(a(5)\) exactly. Since \(\sqrt2>0\), comparison with \(5/\sqrt2\) can be made after multiplying by \(\sqrt2\). We have
\[
\frac72\leq \frac5{\sqrt2}<\frac92.
\]
For the left inequality, it is enough to show
\[
\frac72\sqrt2\leq5.
\]
Both sides are nonnegative, and their squares are respectively
\[
\left(\frac72\sqrt2\right)^2=\frac{49}{2}\leq25=5^2.
\]
For the right inequality, it is enough to show
\[
5<\frac92\sqrt2.
\]
Again both sides are nonnegative, and
\[
5^2=25<\frac{81}{2}=
\left(\frac92\sqrt2\right)^2.
\]
Adding \(1/2\) to the displayed bounds gives
\[
4\leq \frac5{\sqrt2}+\frac12<5.
\]
Consequently,
\[
a(5)=\left\lfloor\frac5{\sqrt2}+\frac12\right\rfloor=4.
\]

Similarly,
\[
\frac52\leq \frac4{\sqrt2}<\frac72.
\]
Indeed, the left inequality follows from
\[
\left(\frac52\sqrt2\right)^2= rac{25}{2}\leq16=4^2,
\]
and the right inequality follows from
\[
4^2=16<\frac{49}{2}=
\left(\frac72\sqrt2\right)^2.
\]
All quantities being compared are nonnegative, so these squared comparisons imply the original comparisons. Adding \(1/2\) yields
\[
3\leq \frac4{\sqrt2}+\frac12<4,
\]
and hence
\[
a(4)=\left\lfloor\frac4{\sqrt2}+\frac12\right\rfloor=3.
\]
It follows that the natural-number difference at position \(5\) is
\[
a(5)-a(4)=4-3=1.
\]

It remains to prove that \(5\) is not in the nonhomogeneous Beatty sequence \(\{\lfloor k\phi\rfloor:k\geq1\}\). Suppose, to the contrary, that some positive integer \(k\) satisfies
\[
\lfloor k\phi\rfloor=5.
\]
Since \(k\phi\geq0\), there is no issue from viewing the floor as a natural number. The defining property of the floor then gives
\[
5\leq k\phi<6. \tag{1}
\]
Every integer \(k\) falls into one of the two exhaustive cases \(k\leq3\) or \(k\geq4\).

If \(k\leq3\), then \(\phi>0\), so
\[
k\phi\leq3\phi.
\]
But
\[
3\phi=\frac32(1+\sqrt5)<5.
\]
To see the strict inequality, note that
\[
\sqrt5<\frac73,
\]
because both sides are positive and
\[
5<\frac{49}{9}.
\]
Thus
\[
3\phi=\frac32(1+\sqrt5)
 <\frac32\left(1+\frac73\right)=5.
\]
Hence \(k\phi<5\), contradicting the left inequality in (1).

If \(k\geq4\), positivity of \(\phi\) gives
\[
k\phi\geq4\phi.
\]
Moreover,
\[
4\phi=2+2\sqrt5>6,
\]
because \(\sqrt5>2\), which follows by squaring from \(5>4\). Therefore \(k\phi>6\), contradicting the right inequality in (1).

Both possibilities for \(k\) lead to contradictions. Thus
\[
5\neq\lfloor k\phi\rfloor
\qquad\text{for every integer }k\geq1.
\]
In other words, \(5\notin A001954\).

We have therefore found \(n=5\geq1\) such that
\[
a(5)-a(4)=1
\]
while \(5\) is not of the form \(\lfloor k\phi\rfloor\) for any \(k\geq1\). This directly contradicts the conjectured equivalence between a difference of \(1\) and membership in A001954. Since that equivalence is one conjunct of the stated conjecture, the entire conjecture is false, independently of whether its inequalities involving \(s(m)\) or its separate characterization of the zero differences hold.
